subtopic: An unrealistic deadline from a manager
subtype: Approach: written follow-up to record the agreement [Action]
passage: Harsha, you asked why I email after every meeting. It started with a mistake. I'm Minakshi. When I was a young woman of twenty-five, my manager and I agreed that the reports would wait until phase two. We shook hands, and nothing was written. Three months later the director asked why the reports were missing, and my manager said I had promised them. I had no proof. The next time, I went straight back to my desk and wrote four lines: what we agreed, what is postponed, and why. "Please tell me if I have misunderstood." The reply came in ten minutes: "Correct." That short email saved me in the next argument as well.

qa.q: What did Minakshi put in the short email?
qa.a: The email said what we agreed, what is postponed, and why.

qa.q: How did Minakshi feel when the director asked about the missing reports?
qa.a: Minakshi felt cornered and worried, having no proof of what had been agreed.

qa.q: Which choice in the story protected Minakshi, and why?
qa.a: Writing the summary right after the meeting and inviting a correction protected Minakshi, because it created a record the manager had confirmed.

qa.q: How might the manager have seen the short email?
qa.a: The manager probably found it clear and fair, since it invited a correction and needed only one word to confirm.

grounding: Illustrates emailing the manager a short summary of what was agreed and deferred and why, to avoid later disputes about what was promised.

subtopic: An unrealistic deadline from a manager

passage:
The meeting with her manager had run until seven, and the office lights in the Gurugram tower were switching off floor by floor. Indu had one more thing to do before the cab came in fifteen minutes.
They had agreed a lot in that hour. The core payment flow would ship on the 30th. Refunds and reports would move to next month because the bank's test system wasn't ready. Indu's team would get one extra tester for two weeks.
Her colleague Reena, packing up, asked, "Aren't you going home?"
"In a minute. If I don't write this down tonight, in a month everyone will remember it differently."
She typed quickly: "Hi Vikram, thanks for today. Summary of what we agreed: 1. Core payment flow ships 30th. 2. Refunds and reports deferred to next month, because the bank test system is unavailable. 3. One extra tester for two weeks from Monday. Please correct me if I've missed anything."
She hit send as the cab pulled up.

qa.q: When will the core payment flow ship?
qa.a: The core payment flow will ship on the 30th.

qa.q: Why did Indu stay to write the email, and how did she feel?
qa.a: She was worried that everyone would remember the agreement differently later, so she felt it was worth staying even though she was tired.

qa.q: What else could Indu do if Vikram replies with a correction?
qa.a: She could update the summary and resend it, so the final written version is the one everyone agrees on.

qa.q: How might Reena see Indu's late email?
qa.a: Reena may think it's extra effort at the end of a long day, but could see why a written record avoids arguments later.

grounding: Shows the person emailing the manager a short summary after a deadline discussion, listing what was agreed, what was deferred and why.

subtopic: An unrealistic deadline from a manager
subtype: Approach: written follow-up to record the agreement [Action]
passage:
Amandeep came out of her manager's cabin in the Andheri office with a head full of agreements. The deadline talk had gone well: the checkout feature would go live on 10 June, the discount-code module would wait for July because the pricing team hadn't finished its rules, and she could borrow Kunal from the web team for a week.
Kunal caught her at the coffee machine. "So I'm on your team next week?"
"Yes. And I'm writing it down now."
She sat at her desk and wrote an email to her manager: "Thanks for the discussion. To confirm: checkout goes live 10 June. Discount codes move to July, as pricing rules are not final. Kunal joins for the week of 27 May. Please let me know if I've got anything wrong."
She copied Kunal.
In July, when a sales head asked why discount codes hadn't launched in June, the manager simply forwarded her email. The question ended there.

qa.q: When would the checkout feature go live?
qa.a: It would go live on 10 June.

qa.q: How did Amandeep feel coming out of the cabin?
qa.a: She felt pleased the talk had gone well, but with a head full of agreements she wanted to pin down.

qa.q: What else could Amandeep do with the summary email?
qa.a: She could save it with the project plan, so anyone joining later can see what was agreed and why.

qa.q: How did the email help the manager in July?
qa.a: The manager could simply forward it to the sales head, avoiding a dispute about what had been promised.

grounding: Shows the person emailing the manager a short summary of what was agreed, deferred and why, which later settles a question about promises.
